The Arrival

It has stood here
since before the columns
were raised.

Neo-Georgian. Longitudinal plan. Columned portico. Circular drive. The proportions are correct because the original drawings survived.

Built by Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen.

The same men
who built Pinehurst.

The Threshold

The door has been open
since 1916.

Original leaded glass sidelights and over-door fanlight at the front entry, preserved exactly as built. The hardware was specified in 1916. It has not been replaced.

That is not maintenance. That is devotion.

The Interior

You are inside
before you have processed
what you walked into.

The foyer runs the full depth of the house. Original oak floors. Two primary stair cores. The axis was drawn in 1915. Restored 1999–2001 by Thomas O'Shea.

Nothing has been changed that didn't need to be.

The Drawing Room

Fire going.
No one home yet.

The Delft-tiled fireplace is original. Formal by proportion. Intimate by firelight. Seven fireplaces in this house. This is the one you come back to.

The Library

You cannot leave
this room quickly.

The books change. The shelves do not. Original oak millwork. Tennessee marble. The light comes from the east and stays longer than it should.

Seven rooms. Seven fireplaces. One house that has never forgotten who it is.

The Primary Suite

Three Jacuzzi tubs.
A balcony over the garden.
Morning light from the east.

The bedroom opens to a private balcony above the grounds. Dressing room. Three full baths. The suite was designed for someone who intended to stay.

The History

He named it Garran Hill.
He longed for it every day
he was gone.

He bought the land in February 1913. He commissioned the design. He directed the craftsmen. Walter Hines Page — publisher, ambassador, son of the South — never slept here. He died on December 21, 1918, before the house was finished.

Walter Hines Page  ·  1855 – 1918

Publisher. Ambassador.
The man who named
this hill.

Editor of The Atlantic. Co-founder of Doubleday. U.S. Ambassador to Great Britain during the First World War. He carried a letter of introduction from Woodrow Wilson and the homesickness of a man who had built something beautiful on Carolina soil that he would never see finished.

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"

In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.

The Grounds

4.15 acres.
The world outside
does not exist here.

Salt water pool, 20 × 40 feet, installed 2022. Rose garden. Mature boxwood. Twenty-eight irrigation zones fed by a 130-foot well. Twelve parking spaces. The canopy took 110 years to grow.

Betty Dumaine called her horse Blue Fox. He is buried here, beneath a slate cover with a brass marker.

Someone still puts flowers there.

It is ready for
the fifth family.
